{"id": "75:40/q08", "question": "How difficult is revival compared with first creation?", "turns_on": "The notes distinguish rational comparison between first and second creation from equality of all acts for divine power.", "positions": [{"id": "75:40/q08/p1", "position": "Revival is easier by rational comparison with originating life.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr calls this the more famous of two views and relates the debate to 30:27. Al-Bursevī reasons that primordial matter and original elements remain. Al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī argue from the completed first creation. Al-Biqāʿī compares forming two sexes from one drop with separating a dead person's dust from earth."}, {"id": "75:40/q08/p2", "position": "The two acts are equal in divine power, even if revival seems harder to people.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports equality as the other view in the argument about 30:27. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says reviving the dead can seem harder than reshaping fingertips to human reason, although divine acts are equal."}]}
{"id": "75:40/q09", "question": "Why is this final resurrection question so emphatic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:40/q09/p1", "position": "Its full interrogative and emphatic bāʾ give resurrection more rhetorical weight than the shorter affirmation of shaping fingertips.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts the explicit balā qādirīn about fingertips, where verb and circumstantial subject are omitted, with this complete question; human reason can see revival as harder. He says the two passages pair God's power over fingertips and over the dead, affirming the former directly and the latter interrogatively."}]}
{"id": "75:40/q10", "question": "What is reported as the response when this verse is recited?", "turns_on": "The reports give distinct affirmative formulas, some adding glorification, testimony, divine might, or a direct declaration of ability.", "positions": [{"id": "75:40/q10/p1", "position": "Glorify or praise God and affirm yes; the transmitted invocations vary.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, al-Barāʾ, Abū Hurayra, Abū Jaʿfar, Abū ʿAbd Allāh, al-Riḍā, and reports from the Prophet supply forms such as subḥānaka Allāhumma wa-balā, subḥānahu wa-balā, subḥāna rabbī wa-balā, and praise with assent. Some add 'by God' twice or 'Lord of the worlds'; al-Wāḥidī reports 'Our Lord, yes.' Rooftop and prayer reports attribute this response to the Prophet; Ibn Kathīr says Abū Dāwūd alone transmits the rooftop report and its unnamed Companion does not harm it. Ibn ʿAbbās says to answer even while leading prayer, comparing the response at 87:1."}, {"id": "75:40/q10/p2", "position": "Answer simply 'yes' (balā).", "reasons": "The Prophet is reported to do this and to instruct reciters through Abū Hurayra and Jābir; Ibn ʿAbbās also teaches assent. The Abū Hurayra instruction pairs 75:40 with 95:8 and 77:50, giving the latter their own answers. Ibn Kathīr names Abū Dāwūd, Aḥmad, and al-Tirmidhī as transmitters; al-Ḥākim authenticates one version, while al-Haythamī notes two unknown men in Aḥmad's chain. Al-Suyūṭī also cites the instruction and separately notes that seven of twenty-two Qur'anic occurrences of balā cannot be paused on because following words are syntactically attached; his count concerns Qur'anic balā generally."}, {"id": "75:40/q10/p3", "position": "Answer 'yes, and I am among those who testify.'", "reasons": "Abū Umāma reports hearing the Prophet frequently recite the sūra and use this response."}, {"id": "75:40/q10/p4", "position": "Answer 'yes, by the might of our Lord.'", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī attributes this version of the closing response to al-Tirmidhī."}, {"id": "75:40/q10/p5", "position": "Answer 'O God, indeed You are able.'", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī reports Ibn ʿAbbās prescribing this answer to whoever recites the verse."}, {"id": "75:40/q10/p6", "position": "Answer 'subḥānaka Allāhumma, qabli.'", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim records this wording both from a reciter who heard the Prophet and from Ibn ʿAbbās himself."}]}
{"id": "75:40/q11", "question": "What promise is reported for a reciter who believes this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:40/q11/p1", "position": "The Prophet and Gabriel will testify on Resurrection Day that the reciter believed in it.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī attributes this promise to the Prophet and gives no grading."}]}
{"id": "75:40/q12", "question": "How does this ending connect to the sūra's opening and argument?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "75:40/q12/p1", "position": "It returns to the opening doubt about resurrection and completes the argument from human creation.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī joins the opening collection of bones to resurrection on the Day of Gathering. Iṣlāḥī links 75:3–4 and the question whether humanity is left unaccountable, which he says would violate divine justice and wisdom. Al-Sāmarrāʾī links the opening oath, gathered bones, record of deeds, threats in 75:34–35, omitted agents in the creation account, and the closing resurrection proof. Kur'an Yolu notes the warning after human creation; Ibn ʿĀshūr says 75:37–40 prepare the closing question and echo 21:104."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q01", "question": "What does the emphatic assertion of divine revelation establish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q01/p1", "position": "God Himself and no one else truly sent the Qur’an to Muhammad; the repeated pronoun reinforces that certainty against denial and reassures him.", "reasons": "Kashshāf says the repeated pronoun doubles emphasis on God's exclusive action and assures the Prophet that staged revelation follows wisdom; its commands of patience now and fighting later come from the wise author of every act. Rāzī says the unbelievers' charges of soothsaying and magic made such confirmation and consolation necessary; the Lord of the heavens honors His Messenger despite slander. Qurṭubī denies that Muhammad invented the book and says it is truth rather than magic, soothsaying, or poetry. Bayḍāwī and Nasafī stress the doubled pronoun and God's sole agency; Nasafī links this to purposeful gradual revelation and perseverance. Qāshānī says God Himself, without another. Biqāʿī sees God's limitless greatness in the doubled assertion and says it answers strong rejection while followers await permission to fight. Bursawī cites Meccan charges of sorcery and soothsaying and urges the Prophet not to heed them. Elmalılı also stresses God's sole agency. Ālūsī says emphatic pronouns reinforce the claim of gradual revelation. Sāmarrāʾī counts three markers of emphasis that name sender, message, and recipient: Quraysh denied revelation strongly though they acknowledged God as creator (31:25; 39:38), and the worship-giving book serves creation's purpose (51:56). He compares Yā Sīn's stronger assertion and oath after the rejection of a third messenger (36:14, 36:16)."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q02", "question": "How is نحن parsed in the sentence?", "turns_on": "Whether نحن depends on the pronoun of إن, separates subject and predicate, or heads its own clause; Samīn disputes describing a pronoun by a pronoun.", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q02/p1", "position": "It is an accusative dependent of the pronoun in إن, serving emphasis; Makkī calls it an adjective.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās allows an accusative adjective. Samīn reports emphasis of the noun of إن and reports Makkī's adjective analysis, but objects that one pronoun does not describe another and that Makkī's account amounts to emphasis."}, {"id": "76:23/q02/p2", "position": "It is a separating pronoun, while نزلنا supplies the predicate of إن.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās and Samīn both offer this parse; Samīn states that نزلنا itself is the predicate of إن on this analysis."}, {"id": "76:23/q02/p3", "position": "It is a nominative subject whose predicate is نزلنا, with the resulting clause serving as the predicate of إن.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās gives the subject-and-predicate parse; Samīn specifies that this complete clause predicates إن."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q03", "question": "Why say عليك here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q03/p1", "position": "The address to the Prophet suits the commands that follow.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī contrasts al-Ḥijr 15:9, which centers on the Qur’an without a surrounding address to him, with the direct commands in 76:24–26."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q04", "question": "How is القرآن read with respect to its hamza?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q04/p1", "position": "The canonical Ḥamza reading elides the hamza, yielding Qurān without a change of meaning.", "reasons": "QIRAAT-ER describes this as simplifying the glottal stop."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q05", "question": "Why is the revelation called القرآن here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q05/p1", "position": "This is the sūra's only use of Qur’an for the revelation; al-Ḥijr uses dhikr to answer Quraysh's own wording and fit its preceding verse.", "reasons": "Sāmarrāʾī compares 15:6 and 15:9."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q06", "question": "What purpose or effect does the revealed Qur’an have?", "turns_on": "The notes give different stated functions and effects of the revelation, without arguing that they exclude one another.", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q06/p1", "position": "It gives people needed guidance, guards against deviation, and heals spiritual disorders.", "reasons": "Qurṭubī says the book contains what people need and is true. Biqāʿī attributes its comprehensive guidance to the revealer's encompassing knowledge and power and says its knowledge and practice heal spiritual disorders. Elmalılı says it guides humanity to the right path and offers the delight of the pure drink."}, {"id": "76:23/q06/p2", "position": "God sent it as a trial and test.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī states this purpose."}, {"id": "76:23/q06/p3", "position": "It will bring about further events, and what is promised will certainly occur.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says the revelation has consequences beyond those already mentioned

."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q07", "question": "How did the Qur’an come down, and why in that manner?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q07/p1", "position": "It came in successive portions rather than all at once, at appointed times governed by divine wisdom.", "reasons": "Qushayrī says over years; Ibn ʿAbbās, cited by Baghawī and Qurṭubī, says verse after verse, not all at once; Ibn al-Jawzī also says separate installments. Kashshāf relates stages to wisdom and the sequence of patience now, fighting and retribution later. Rāzī says every matter has its appointed time and the Prophet should accept the wise, faultless decree patiently. Bayḍāwī and Bursawī cite the wisdom requiring stages. Nasafī connects stages with purposeful perseverance. Biqāʿī says stages answer questions and ease people step by step into religious duties. Ālūsī and Elmalılı specify about twenty-three years; Elmalılı compares gradual revelation to the first human's stages of creation. Asad says the verbal form nazzalnā implies gradualness. Study Quran reports JJ and Ṭs's installment reading."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q08", "question": "What is the grammatical force of تنزيلا?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q08/p1", "position": "It is an emphatic verbal noun.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās explicitly calls tanzīlan emphatic."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q09", "question": "How does this verse follow the earlier account of humanity and its outcomes?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q09/p1", "position": "The sūra moves from human creation, trial, guidance, and divergent outcomes to the gift and truth of revelation for the Prophet.", "reasons": "Rāzī traces the opening from nonexistence and the mixtures of 76:1, understood variously as elements, humors, parental fluids, body and spirit or soul, and embryonic stages; these point to a freely choosing Creator. He says humanity was made for trial, supplied with hearing, sight, and especially reason, and guided to a path (76:2–3). He notes punishment is brief but reward extensive, then says 76:22 completes the afterlife subject before worldly duties. Qurṭubī says the prior promises and threats lead to affirmation that the book is true and meets people's needs. Biqāʿī recalls guidance, grateful believers, deniers, and their outcomes, comparing the pure drink that revives dead earth to Qur’anic knowledge reviving dead hearts. Ālūsī says the account of obedient and disobedient people and mercy for the obedient leads to honor for the Prophet to ease loneliness. KURANYOLU describes the preceding afterlife outcomes as corresponding to worldly beliefs and deeds."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q10", "question": "What does the different amount of space given to punishment and reward show?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q10/p1", "position": "Mercy is stronger and more prevalent.", "reasons": "Rāzī infers this from the brief treatment of punishment and lengthy description of reward through 76:22."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q11", "question": "How does this verse prepare the commands that follow?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q11/p1", "position": "The honor and reassurance of revelation strengthen the Prophet for patient obedience, worship, and perseverance amid opponents.", "reasons": "Muqātil connects this to the earlier command to be patient with God's judgment. Rāzī says the Messenger, as head of the obedient community, is reassured before commands and prohibitions; removing harm precedes gaining benefit, so prohibitions come first. His account of the sūra's arrangement includes its opening, this reassurance, commands, and later rebels. He says accusations made the Prophet lonely and that patience is commanded despite his wish to fight tormentors until wise revelation permits it; after revelation and guidance he must obey God alone. Kashshāf and Nasafī likewise connect staged revelation to present patience and later action. Biqāʿī says followers await permission to fight and says revelation honors the Prophet now before the next life, in gratitude for his good conduct and avoidance of impurity before prophethood. Ālūsī says the gift eases loneliness and strengthens his heart. Iṣlāḥī urges trust, prayer, remembrance, and perseverance; KURANYOLU says the reminder of revelation's value steels worship and obedience against deniers. Sāmarrāʾī points to the direct commands in 76:24–26."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q12", "question": "What can the gift of revelation lead people to know about God?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q12/p1", "position": "People can know divine names and attributes and are called to obey God alone, but their minds cannot reach the divine essence.", "reasons": "Rāzī connects this distinction to the Prophet's command after the gift of revelation and guidance."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q13", "question": "Why do deniers resist the revelation and its call?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q13/p1", "position": "They are unwilling to give up immediate gains for the Hereafter and therefore fabricate objections.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says the Hereafter is certain and that God can easily recreate them."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q14", "question": "How is the sūra connected with the one before it?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q14/p1", "position": "Their relationship is clear.", "reasons": "Ālūsī describes it as perfectly clear and mentions 75:40 without further detail in this note."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q15", "question": "What does the sūra's opening say about the division into grateful and ungrateful people?", "turns_on": "Whether gratefulness and ingratitude are assigned to human choice or to God.", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q15/p1", "position": "The division results from people's own choice.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this as the Qadarī reading of 76:3, after the creation, trial, faculties, and guidance of 76:1–3."}, {"id": "76:23/q15/p2", "position": "The division is attributed to God.", "reasons": "Rāzī reports this as the Jabrī reading of 76:3."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q16", "question": "Where was the sūra, or its final section, revealed?", "turns_on": "Whether the whole sūra or only particular later verses are Meccan or Medinan; the two mixed reports differ in how much of the closing section they assign to Mecca.", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q16/p1", "position": "The sūra is Meccan.", "reasons": "Nasafī classifies the whole sūra as Meccan; Ālūsī reports that most authorities cited in al-Baḥr do so."}, {"id": "76:23/q16/p2", "position": "The sūra is wholly Medinan.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports Mujāhid and Qatāda for this view; Ibn ʿĀdil calls an unrestricted Medinan classification the majority view and attributes it also to Shīʿa authorities."}, {"id": "76:23/q16/p3", "position": "The sūra is Medinan except 76:24, which is Meccan.", "reasons": "Ālūsī attributes this report to al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima, and al-Kalbī."}, {"id": "76:23/q16/p4", "position": "The opening section is Medinan, while the closing patient command or commands are Meccan.", "reasons": "Ālūsī reports a version locating the closing command to be patient in Mecca. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the commands to patience and refusal to obey sinners or unbelievers form a later self-contained section that may have been revealed in Mecca, while the opening concerning the Prophet's household was Medinan; the reported extent of the Meccan closing material varies."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q17", "question": "What other names are given to this sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q17/p1", "position": "It is also called al-Dahr, al-Abrār, al-Amshāj, and Hal Atā.", "reasons": "Ālūsī lists these names for Sūrat al-Insān."}]}
{"id": "76:23/q18", "question": "How many verses does the sūra have?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "76:23/q18/p1", "position": "Thirty-one verses.", "reasons": "Nasafī gives this count. Ālūsī, reporting Ibn ʿĀdil, says there is no disagreement about it."}]}
{"id": "79:20/q01", "question": "How does the fāʾ connect the showing to the preceding command?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:20/q01/p1", "position": "It follows an omitted account of Moses going to Pharaoh before showing the sign.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī supply 'he went' after the command; both compare the omitted striking before the rock split in 2:60. Al-Ālūsī says the fuller narrative allows more intervening events than al-Zamakhsharī supplies. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies that Moses went, called Pharaoh, was rejected, and showed the sign; Ṭabāṭabāʾī supplies his coming and calling him. Ibn ʿĀshūr and Ṭabāṭabāʾī call the fāʾ explanatory."}]}
{"id": "79:20/q02", "question": "What does Moses' showing of the sign entail?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:20/q02/p1", "position": "He made Pharaoh see the sign or acquainted him with it.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī gives both senses for the verb and says Pharaoh recognized the sign on seeing it."}]}
{"id": "79:20/q03", "question": "Why are the signs attributed to Moses as the one who showed them?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:20/q03/p1", "position": "Moses is their apparent agent, while God is their true source.", "reasons": "Bursevī contrasts the outward attribution here with God's attribution of the signs to Himself in 20:56. Al-Ālūsī makes the same distinction and cites God's 'We showed him Our signs' in 20:42."}]}
{"id": "79:20/q04", "question": "What does āya mean in this verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:20/q04/p1", "position": "It is a miraculous sign and proof that Moses was God's messenger.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī calls it the supreme miracle; al-Ṭabarī a great proof of prophethood; Ibn Kathīr powerful and clear evidence of a message from God; al-Biqāʿī a sign proving Moses' message after Pharaoh demanded proof. Ibn ʿĀshūr traces āya from sign or marker to evidence establishing truth and then a messenger's miracle. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says religious usage can prove God's existence, greatness, unity, or power or support a chosen messenger, and here

supports Moses' mission."}]}
{"id": "79:20/q05", "question": "Why is āya used with the definite article?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:20/q05/p1", "position": "The noun must be definite here; an indefinite form is not permissible.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says the term cannot occur here without the article or as an indefinite noun."}]}
{"id": "79:20/q06", "question": "What was the great sign shown to Pharaoh?", "turns_on": "The accounts and comparative force of Moses' miracles: some single out the staff or hand, some join them or all the miracles as one proof; others read the sign beyond those miracles. Al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī appeal to the narrative sequence against the collective reading.", "positions": [{"id": "79:20/q06/p1", "position": "Moses' staff, especially its transformation into a serpent.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd calls it the staff and serpent. ʿAṭāʾ says the hand changed color, whereas the staff became alive, grew, swallowed objects, then returned to its former lifeless form. Al-Bayḍāwī calls the serpent the first and central miracle; Abū Ḥayyān, Ibn ʿAbbās as cited by al-Ālūsī, and al-Zamakhsharī make the hand secondary. Bursevī says the sequence makes it first and the other miracles lesser. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī favors the detailed account; Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Pharaoh's demand and the ensuing staff miracle in 26:30–32. Elmalılı sees proof of resurrection and the creative command 'Be.' Iṣlāḥī says the other miracles, apart from the white hand, were contained in and manifested through the staff. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports an argument that its change into a living, powerful thing surpasses a color change. The Study Quran cites 7:107, 20:66–67, and 26:32, 44–45. The wordings 'staff,' 'staff and serpent,' and 'staff becoming a serpent' describe this same identification."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p2", "position": "Moses' staff and shining white hand together count as the great sign.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan, Qatāda, Mujāhid, and the majority of commentators are reported for both signs. Al-Ṭabarī describes the white hand and staff becoming a manifest serpent; Qatāda calls them two signs. Muqātil says the hand shone like the sun without leprosy, dazzling the eye. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says they were displayed in challenge and defeated the false party. Al-Rāzī reports Mujāhid's sequence, staff first and then hand. Al-Nasafī says the pair counts as one sign; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Ālūsī, and al-Zamakhsharī as reported by Bint al-Shāṭiʾ make the hand subsidiary, with their combined proof counting as one. Al-Ālūsī notes that the two are called plural in 20:42 because each contains multiple clear wonders for rational people."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p3", "position": "Moses' shining white hand alone was the great sign.", "reasons": "Al-Qu­shayrī and al-Ṭabrisī compare its brilliance to the sun; al-Qu­shayrī reports that Pharaoh then consulted Haman. Muqātil says it was more wondrous than the staff, dazzling yet free of leprosy. Al-Rāzī reports Maqātil and al-Kalbī citing 27:12 and 20:23; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports exegetes' appeal to 20:23 calling it one of the greatest signs. The Study Quran cites 7:108, 26:33, and 27:12."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p4", "position": "All of Moses' miracles collectively were one great sign.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī say their shared evidentiary force permits a singular sign; al-Ālūsī also mentions referring to the group through its first instance. Kur'an Yolu specifies all nine and cites 7:107–108, 7:133–136, and 17:101. Al-Ālūsī argues against this reading: the magicians were gathered only after the staff and hand, while the remaining nine signs came after their defeat over roughly twenty years (7:133). Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls it remote on the detailed account."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p5", "position": "The sign was the parting of the sea.", "reasons": "The Study Quran cites 7:136, 10:90, 20:77–78, and 26:63–66; al-Qurṭubī and Kur'an Yolu also report this identification."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p6", "position": "The verse leaves the great sign unidentified.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers the Qur'an's choice to call it 'the great sign' and stresses its proof of Moses and God's power. The Study Quran notes that the account of nine clear signs in 17:101 does not select a greatest one."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p7", "position": "It refers to Paradise and Hell.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī reports this from al-Suddī."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p8", "position": "It was God's speech to Moses from the tree.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī offers this as a third possibility."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p9", "position": "It was the true identity disclosed by intellectual unity and divine guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says Pharaoh's veil and delusion prevented recognition of a higher station."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p10", "position": "It was God's guidance offered even to Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Asad calls it measureless grace offered to even the most recalcitrant sinner."}, {"id": "79:20/q06/p11", "position": "It was ʿAlī appearing to Moses in a transformed spiritual state.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes this claim to extremist Shīʿīs and rejects it as irrational and unsupported by transmitted tradition."}]}
{"id": "79:20/q07", "question": "How does the feminine superlative al-kubrā function grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:20/q07/p1", "position": "Though originally adjectival, this form can function as a noun.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān compares al-quṣwā and al-kubrā and gives al-abṭaḥ, al-ajraʿ, and al-adham as other adjectives used substantively."}]}
{"id": "79:20/q08", "question": "Why is this sign called great or greatest?", "turns_on": "The notes compare the hand's brilliance and 20:23 with the staff's greater transformation, or take 'great' as a description of the sign's power as proof or of a collective miracle.", "positions": [{"id": "79:20/q08/p1", "position": "The word magnifies the force of the proof for Moses' mission.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the epithet strengthens the sign's evidentiary support and turns to Moses' call in Ṭā Hā, citing 20:12 and 20:17–18."}, {"id": "79:20/q08/p2", "position": "The staff was greatest because its transformations surpassed the hand's color change.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ says it came alive, grew, swallowed objects, then lost life and form; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reports the same comparison in terms of life and power in an inanimate thing. Al-Bayḍāwī calls it the first and central miracle; Bursevī contrasts it with lesser later signs."}, {"id": "79:20/q08/p3", "position": "The hand was greater for its dazzling radiance or the Qur'anic description of it.", "reasons": "Muqātil says the hand shone like the sun, dazzled the eye, and was more wondrous than the staff without being leprous. {"id": "79:27/q03", "question": "What does the comparison in أَشَدُّ خَلْقًا seek to establish?", "turns_on": "Whether the comparison answers denial of resurrection, concerns workmanship, or establishes the original creation of humans; al-Wahidi and al-Razi argue against the latter alternatives.", "positions": [{"id": "79:27/q03/p1", "position": "Creating the greater heaven shows that God can recreate people after death; the comparison measures difficulty only from the human viewpoint.", "reasons": "Muqatil asks weaker humans to consider their fate and invokes the sky's splitting in 82:1 and 84:1. {"id": "79:27/q08", "question": "What does بَنَىٰهَا say God did to heaven?", "turns_on": "Whether building emphasizes elevation, assembly, even formation, or fitness for angels; some sources combine these descriptions rather than oppose them.", "positions": [{"id": "79:27/q08/p1", "position": "He raised the heaven above earth as a lofty roof or building.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari calls it a roof for earth; al-Thalabi, al-Qurtubi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Tabrisi, and al-Biqai likewise emphasize height or shelter. Al-Wahidi reports commentators calling samk the roof or ceiling. {"id": "79:27/q10", "question": "Does بَنَىٰهَا start a new sentence or modify ٱلسَّمَآءُ?", "turns_on": "The pause after heaven or after built it, the possibility of an omitted relative, and whether a relative description implies an unbuilt heaven or avoids unjoined descriptions.", "positions": [{"id": "79:27/q10/p1", "position": "The question ends at heaven; He built it starts a new sentence explaining how heaven was made.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi reports al-Kisai's pause, al-Farra's exposition, and al-Zajjaj's expanded comparison; he prefers the pause because heaven is not a relative antecedent.
